inlineContent.text: Set up ESPSwift, create a project from its Xcode template, and run it on an ESP32 board. Then change what the firmware does, and test that change on your Mac, without the board.

You need a Mac with Xcode, and a board with a RISC-V based ESP32: an ESP32-C2, C3, C5, C6, C61, H2 or P4, such as the ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1. This tutorial uses that board; for another, choose it when you create the project.
ESPSwift is a command-line tool,

, with an Xcode template. Setting it up installs what Embedded Swift on the ESP32 needs: ESP-IDF, Espressif’s framework for the chip, with its compilers and tools, and a Swift toolchain with Embedded Swift for RISC-V.
Install
with Homebrew, from ESPSwift’s tap. Homebrew asks you to trust taps other than its own: ESPSwift’s, and Espressif’s, whose ESP-IDF Installation Manager (EIM) installs ESP-IDF.
Run
. It installs ESP-IDF, the Swift toolchain and the tools they need, and asks whether to install the Xcode template: answer yes. It takes 5 to 10 minutes, the first time.
Run
to check that everything is in order. It lists what it checked, and tells you how to fix anything that isn’t.
Restart Xcode, so it finds the template.
A project from the template is a firmware that runs on its own: the Blink example blinks the board’s LED. You choose your board when you create it, which sets the chip, the LED and the flash size.
In Xcode, choose File ▸ New ▸ Project. Under Other, choose
ESP32 RISC-V

Xcode builds the firmware with ESP-IDF, flashes it to the board over USB, and shows what the board prints in its console.
Connect the board to your Mac. On the ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1, use its port labelled
USB
, the chip’s own USB port, which also lets you debug the firmware later.

Press Cmd+B to build the firmware. The first build takes a few minutes, as it builds ESP-IDF too; later ones take seconds. Errors appear in the Issue navigator, linked to their line, as for any project.
Xcode’s run destination says My Mac: Xcode runs
on your Mac, which flashes the board.
Press Cmd+R. Xcode flashes the firmware to the board and shows its output in the console: the board restarts, the firmware says hello, and the LED blinks red, green, blue and off.
Press Cmd+. to stop watching the console. The firmware keeps running on the board, also without the Mac: connect it to any USB power supply.
Change the firmware, and run it again. Code completion works as in any Swift project, after the first build, for Swift and for ESP-IDF’s C APIs.
Change what the firmware says when it starts.
Press Cmd+R to see the change on the board.
Make the LED blink four times as fast: wait 250 milliseconds instead of 1000.

Open

Add yellow to the pattern: red and green together. The pattern now repeats every 5 steps.
Code in the Kit package runs on the Mac too, so its tests run there, without the board: quick to run, and on any Mac.
Open
. Its tests, with Swift Testing, check the pattern: still red, green, blue and off.
Press Cmd+U. The tests run on the Mac, and fail: the pattern has yellow now, and repeats every 5 steps.
Update the tests for the new pattern, and press Cmd+U again: they pass. Then press Cmd+R to see yellow on the board.

// says which LED the board has, and LED.swift drives it: an addressable RGB
// LED (WS2812), separate red, green and blue LEDs, or a one-colour LED (on for
// any colour). Without an LED, it only prints the colours.
print("\(Board.name) has no LED to blink; printing the colours instead.")
// Cycle through Red, Green, Blue, and Off — one color per second.

// Wait 1 second using FreeRTOS task delay.

content: // This example blinks the board's LED: red, green, blue and off. Board.swift
// says which LED the board has, and LED.swift drives it: an addressable RGB
// LED (WS2812), separate red, green and blue LEDs, or a one-colour LED (on for
// any colour). Without an LED, it only prints the colours.
print("Hello from Embedded Swift on ESP32!")
print("\(Board.name) has no LED to blink; printing the colours instead.")
// Cycle through Red, Green, Blue, and Off — one color per second.
// The color for this step: red, green, blue or off (see Blink.swift).
led?.show(red: step.red, green: step.green, blue: step.blue)
// Wait 1 second using FreeRTOS task delay.
// The blink pattern, in plain Swift: it doesn't use ESP-IDF, so it can be
// tested on the Mac (see Tests/BlinkTests: Cmd+U).
/// One step of the blink pattern: a color for the LED and its name.
/// Cycles through red, green, blue, yellow and off.
///   - index: The step number; the pattern repeats every 5 steps.
///   - brightness: The color's brightness, 0–255. Low by default, as the
public func blinkStep(_ index: UInt32, brightness: UInt32 = 32) -> BlinkStep {
case 0: BlinkStep(red: brightness, green: 0, blue: 0, name: "Red")
case 1: BlinkStep(red: 0, green: brightness, blue: 0, name: "Green")
case 2: BlinkStep(red: 0, green: 0, blue: brightness, name: "Blue")
case 3: BlinkStep(red: brightness, green: brightness, blue: 0, name: "Yellow")
// This example blinks the board's LED: red, green, blue and off. Board.swift
// says which LED the board has, and LED.swift drives it: an addressable RGB
// LED (WS2812), separate red, green and blue LEDs, or a one-colour LED (on for
// any colour). Without an LED, it only prints the colours.
print("\(Board.name) has no LED to blink; printing the colours instead.")
// Cycle through Red, Green, Blue, and Off — one color per second.
// The color for this step: red, green, blue or off (see Blink.swift).
led?.show(red: step.red, green: step.green, blue: step.blue)
// Wait a quarter of a second using FreeRTOS task delay.
